blocks.x: Charles L. Dufor. And date of birth? I was born in New Orleans, January the 17th, 1903. And have you lived here all your life? I lived here all my life. This is being recorded on

the evening of Monday, 12th of May, 1958. When did you first become aware of the second form of music that New Orleans came from? Oh, I would suppose during my college days at QA and I had a QA in 1921. Prior to that, we had,

as a kid growing up, we had, what was known as ragtime. We had ragtime records on the phonograph, along with Carusos and other Red Fields. But the transition of ragtime into jazz took place, I believe, back during my college days, back in the 1921-22 period. Now, you realize you're talking to a non-expert on jazz, and I'm only giving you a recollection that may not be authentic. Well, you say when you were going to high school, when you were going to dance or... Well, I wasn't much of a party boy

during my high school days. I would say what was played in those days was the mainly was what we call still called ragtime. It was I can remember the Tuxedo Band was a famous band. And they played what was genuinely called ragtime all the way down until I think about the 20. That's when the term jazz came into the picture. And just how jazz differed from ragtime as a non-expert, certainly I'm not in a position to tell you. I get that from Fouchon and my Lenville and that group. But I would say that in the evolution of this thing. You know those bands and I like to pat my foot to the music. But I have never the music has never played an important part in my, what shall we say, musical experience. But I've never been opposed. I've never been opposed to it, as I one is opposed to Mr. E. Prepwood. Well, what did people think of it? What if they, you know, parents' contemporaries thought of it? Well, you see, my parents
were quite old when I was born, and my father died in 1913 when I was just 10, and it had hardly emerged as an art farm. And it was just,

they grew up in the opera house, and anything that wasn't operatic music was flat crowd. The same could be true of my mother who lived considerably longer. Did you know anything about your parents' friends? Well, I was hardly at 10 years old, know any of the habits of my father's friends. And of course, your own great-grandmother was a good friend of my mother's, Mrs. Waterman, lived right behind us. And I remember going to the old French opera with Mrs. Waterman, my mother, as a little boy. So that's how I can say that I know my mother and Mrs. Waterman didn't go to any jazz parties. So that may answer your question. Well, when you were in high school and college, they tend to have ragtime or jazz bands at most of the parties you went to. They had those, what they called strip dances in those days. And a couple of people would get up a comedian and get up the dances, and everybody paid to get in. The couples would pay. And what they paid paid for the subscription act. I mean, what they paid paid for the band. There were a lot of... This is when you were in college? Well, that was current in college up to my day. I think from my day it began to die out. I'd heard them talk about my predecessors. But a lot of the guys, a lot of the bands about that time were like the 678 band, made up of college boys, or high school boys. I remember one very fine band was Dick Mackey. You've probably heard about Dick Mackey around here. In fact, I think Dick lived on the Gaul. His family lived on the Gulf Coast, where you were. And Dick Mackey had a band. segments.title: Opening, birth in New Orleans, and first awareness of jazz
segments.summary: Dufour gives his birth date and says he has lived in New Orleans all his life; recording date stated. He places first awareness of the new music in his college days.

segments.title: Ragtime records growing up and the shift to jazz; disclaims expertise
segments.summary: He recalls ragtime records on the phonograph, the Tuxedo Band playing ragtime until about 1920, and the term jazz arriving. He cannot say how they differ and defers to Souchon and Menville.

segments.title: Parents, the French Opera, and attitudes to jazz at home
segments.summary: His parents were old, his father died in 1913, and they lived in the opera world where non-operatic music was low. He recalls going to the French Opera with his mother and Mrs. Waterman.

segments.chapter: Dances and bands of his youth
segments.title: College boys' bands and strip dances; Dick Mackey and Negro bands
segments.summary: Subscription dances paid for bands, often made up of college or high school boys such as Dick Mackey's, who worked their way through school. He also names Negro bands like the Tuxedo and Papa Celestin's.

segments.chapter: Dances and bands of his youth
segments.title: Dance music of the Charleston era; ragtime evolved into jazz
segments.summary: Dance bands played popular tunes of the day, with dances taking names from the music. He sees ragtime-to-jazz as evolution and refers to Souchon, Menville and Kennedy as the experts.

segments.title: Whether college bands were true jazz bands; jazz passed him by
segments.summary: Pressed on whether the college bands were bona fide jazz bands, he says he is not competent to define it; jazz passed him by without his opposing or joining it.

segments.title: Jazz meant nothing to him; ballpark bands and the Pelicans
segments.summary: Jazz did not offend him. He recalls a Black band at the ballpark on Sundays in the 1920s playing Maryland roll call, big crowds, and the Pelicans rallies.

segments.title: Hard to date the ragtime-to-jazz transition; hot tunes and colored bands at parties
segments.summary: He cannot pinpoint the change from ragtime to jazz. Parties played the hot tunes of the day, jazzed up from earlier songs; he cannot say whether colored bands were used at debutante parties, and visitors arrive.

segments.title: Not offended by jazz; fondness for Papa Celestin and Souchon's group
segments.summary: He admits he once may have felt jazz was low but now is not offended, though he would not seek it out. He loves Celestin, When the Saints Go Marching In, and Souchon's group.

segments.title: How widely jazz was accepted in New Orleans, and by whom
segments.summary: He thinks most New Orleanians accepted jazz, especially dancers and party-goers, and that devotees were truly enthused. He cannot say what others thought thirty years ago.

segments.title: Jazz as entertainment versus an art form
segments.summary: He thinks people first saw jazz as music to dance to, but gradually it came to be seen as an emerging indigenous New Orleans art form.

segments.title: Interest in jazz since the 1930s; Dixieland and swing
segments.summary: He thinks interest in jazz continued through the 1930s despite derivatives like swing; today's Dixieland is a version of New Orleans jazz. He likens himself to an onlooker unfamiliar with animal husbandry.

segments.title: Is jazz history research a waste of money?
segments.summary: He says many New Orleanians now see worth in jazz, and defends a $75,000 jazz history project as a contribution to New Orleans history.

segments.chapter: Family dates and the opera house
segments.title: Lingering stigma against jazz; acceptance as an art form is growing
segments.summary: He believes some, like a friend with an opera collection, still treat jazz as untouchable, but the divergence is smaller than 30 years ago and more accept it as an art form.

segments.title: Parents' dates and the old French Opera House
segments.summary: He gives his parents' birth and death years and explains his mother attended the French Opera House from childhood until it burned in 1919.
